body: Yes, this is meant to avoid copies and to allow to modify the structure of the tree.

hmm... I guess if we make defensive copies that will hurt performance and disallow to modify the structure
can we fiddle with garbage collection and only allow to remove the object if the refcount on the attributes is one?

What's wrong with actually storing ndarrays that own the data (although you can access them without the numpy indirection by storing a second pointer to their data), and using their `resize` method for reallocation? This would also avoid the memcpy on `__setstate__`.

At the moment I'm exploring a version that stores an array for most node properties, and a separate one for values. I.e.

``` cython
cdef struct Node:
    # Does not store values at node, as shape is not known at compile time
    SIZE_t left_child
    SIZE_t right_child
    SIZE_t feature
    DOUBLE_t threshold
    DOUBLE_t impurity
    SIZE_t n_samples

cdef class Tree:
    ...
    cdef object node_ndarray     # dtype is record; maintains ownership of data
    cdef Node[::contiguous] nodes    # for fast internal use; stride known at compile time
    cdef object value_ndarray    # maintains ownership of data
    cdef double[::, ::1] value    # for fast internal use

    property children_left:
        def __get__(self):
            return self.value_ndarry['left_child']
    ...
```

In any case, I think there at least needs to be a warning in the `Tree` docstring.
The code has been rewritten so as to avoid the use of Numpy arrays. It is meant to skip the overhead due to accessing such arrays.
Hence the contiguous memoryviews, or equivalently a duplicate pointer to the data; but keep an ndarray copy to provide the safety of refcounting.

> Hence the contiguous memoryviews, or equivalently a duplicate pointer to the data; but keep an ndarray copy to provide the safety of refcounting.

Sounds good to me.

One problem I've found in this strategy is that you need the gil to resize a np array (although I haven't looked for a numpy C-API alternative). I assume that's no big deal, given the infrequency and time consumed the operation.

In any case I'm currently benchmarking an alternative implementation of `build` and `predict`. It cuts out 100 lines of Cython. The curves from the benchmarking script aren't very stable because of the random variation in data (which is why I have suggested the new learning curve framework for a more stable benchmark), even when taking best-of-3 of an average of 10 trials at each point. The implementations appear to have roughly the same performance (in accord with the pointer-vs-memoryview benchmarks I've seen):

issue.title: [MRG] ENH/FIX Change Tree underlying data structure
issue.body:
- avoid segfault (#2726) by setting base on numpy arrays
- A struct array for tree nodes and values array (size indeterminate at compile time) are the only underlying structure, so each node is locally grouped memory, and joblib dumps will save only two numpy files per tree.
- `predict` uses the value array's `take` method, reducing code repetition
